doc.title: Bobby Militello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

chapter: Big breaks: New Wave, Maynard, Tony Bennett
title: Maynard Ferguson hears New Wave; Militello gets the baritone chair
summary: Maynard heard the band at the Landmark; Mike Migliore recommended Militello, who borrowed a baritone and bought one at Manny's.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Yeah. And we weren’t making any money at all. I think I made five grand that whole year. And I learned more and broke more plateaus in soloing and the understanding of jazz during that period I think, almost than during any period of my life. We were working at it and we were grooving. Absolutely grooving. And it was a great thing. During that period is when Maynard heard us opening up at the Landmark, which was a big bowling alley, but Maynard was playing in the banquet room here in Buffalo and we were opening up for him and he heard us there. Actually he first needed an alto player so he called Mike Migliore, who was with the band, with New Wave too. So Mike went out there, and not even three months later Bruce Johnstone decided to split. So then Mike calls me up and he says, “Hey man, you want to play with Maynard?” I say well hell yeah. I dreamed about it when I was a kid. Sure I want the gig. He said, “It’s on bari.” I says oh man. All right I’ll do it. So I went and borrowed a bari, because I’d never played bari, I was always alto, tenor, soprano, flute, clarinet. So I borrowed a bari. I knew I could do it. I mean it was a saxophone. So I borrowed a bari and went out and got the gig instantly. So then I went, he said the next tour starts in two weeks in such-and-such New York. So I flew to New York a day early, went to Manny’s. They had two baris, one with a low A and one without. I said I’ll take the one without. Because I hated the low A baris. I hated the balance of the horn. It didn’t play bop real well. It didn’t feel right. So I

bought the one with the B flat. Maynard said that was cool, I didn’t have to worry about it. All the writers hated me because they all wrote low A’s. But that didn’t bother me either. So I started playing bari with Maynard. And that was a childhood dream. That, and playing with Brubeck were both childhood dreams. And so that was really my first big break as far as now playing with someone big. Previous to that in Buffalo here I had gotten to play with/back up Ella Fitzgerald and Tony Bennett. There is one for the books right there. Again, the experiences you’ll never ever forget in your life. I walk in, the section is basically Sedola is in the section but it’s all Sedola students. Tony Carreri, myself, Vic Kyoto, Russell Dielba and somebody else. It was all Sedola students. Okay? I’m playing the tenor chair. This is when “Something” and all those tunes were out, right? That big album that he had. He got “It Don’t Mean a Thing if it Ain’t Got that Swing” and all that stuff. So I got the tenor chair, and I’ve got an alto flute double, a flute double and a clarinet double. Who walks out to conduct us is Torrie Zito. I go well this is poo man. So we start to do the rehearsal and Torrie stops the orchestra and he says, “Who’s the sound technician here?” And the guy raises his hand. He says, “Okay strike every microphone except for the solo microphone for the sax player and for Tony.” What do you mean? He said, “Man, take a break orchestra.” Because this was a full orchestra gig. Take a break. He wants this gig one hundred percent acoustic. And he doesn’t like what the guy — strike everything. So they strike everything off the stage, two mics. Now we come back and we start to play and of course a good conductor is going to play something to find out what the soloist can do. He’s got to know before he gets into the gig. So we’ve started off with “Something.” And I’m sitting in the middle of that orchestra and we start to play the chart and I can barely play because it’s so beautiful and I can hear the changes so clear. I mean every nuance, every moving part I can hear it clear as a bell because it’s acoustic. So I can hear everything from my position. So now he gets up to back up Tony on “Something.” And I start to blow. Can I swear?
